By the end of my first internship year I had a stiff neck, a sore wrist and no energy after six. I'm Irfan, and I'd been coding on a laptop balanced on my bed, eating chips for dinner.
My friend Ojas, a physiotherapy student, came over and winced at my setup. "You're folded like a shrimp."
He didn't lecture me. He just raised the laptop on two old textbooks, found me a chair with a back, and showed me three stretches for my neck. "Every hour, stand up. Walk to the kitchen. Drink water."
I started cycling to the office twice a week and cooking dal and vegetables on Sundays for the next few days.
It took a month before I noticed. My neck stopped hurting. I had energy for the evening cricket game again.

qa.a: Two old textbooks.

qa.a: Irfan felt stiff, sore and drained, with no energy after six.

qa.a: Ojas would likely feel pleased and a bit proud that the small changes made a difference.

Kaito, the senior volunteer, read the file and shook his head. "The law says no."

At the college debating society, held in the old seminar hall, the topic was: "A law is only as good as the people it protects."
Trisha had been assigned to argue against it. Halfway through her speech, she stopped.
"I can't argue this side honestly," she said. "Some laws have been legal and wrong at the same time. Laws have kept people out of temples, out of voting, out of schools. Following them didn't make it right."
The room murmured. The judge, Manjula ma'am, frowned. "You'll lose points."
"I know." Trisha's hands were shaking. "I'd rather lose points than defend something I think is unfair."
She lost the round. Afterwards Manjula ma'am found her. "Next time, argue it by testing it. But I respect the stand."

qa.a: In the old seminar hall.

qa.a: She felt nervous but firm, her hands shaking as she refused to argue something she thought unfair.

Emil joined the Berlin community swimming club as a boy, and now, at twenty, he coached the beginners on Wednesday evenings.
This season a new girl, Zeynep, came with her mother. She was eleven, newly arrived, and afraid of putting her face in the water.

Afterwards the club manager asked Emil if he'd join the committee. He hesitated, then said yes. "Someone did this for me once."

Avni, you ask why I make such a fuss about you voting. Let me tell you.
When I was twenty-one, I didn't bother. It was raining, I had a class, one vote didn't matter. My father went to the booth with his walking stick and came back soaked. He said nothing, but he looked at me, his only daughter.
That same year he fell ill, and I became the one who took him to the hospital, filed his papers and paid our house tax on time, because nobody else would.
Sitting in that government office, I understood: everything we have runs because people turn up and do the dull things.
The next election, I, Ankita, stood in the rain and voted. I took him too, in a wheelchair.
So go, beta. Your vote is not dull.

Thursday night
Nearly did something stupid today. Madhav sent a message in the office group mocking my presentation. My thumbs were already typing something nasty.
Then I stopped. Put the phone face down. Went to the balcony. Watched the traffic for five minutes. My heart was still hammering, but slower.
Two years ago I'd have sent it. I'd have spent a week fixing the mess.
When I came back, I wrote to Madhav privately: "That stung. Can we talk tomorrow?" He replied, "Sorry, it was a bad joke."
I'm proud of the five minutes on the balcony. Not proud of how angry I still get. But the gap between feeling and doing is longer now.

Dear Seema,
Remember how I used to lose my keys twice a day? Here's a funny update.
Last week at the hospital, the senior doctor gave me a verbal handover on six patients in three minutes, each with different medicines and timings, and then got called away. I had no paper. My heart dropped.
But then I did the thing I've been practising: I linked each patient to their bed number and one picture in my head. Bed 3, the lady with the red shawl, sugar check at eight. Bed 5, the young man with the cast, painkiller at nine.
I wrote it all down in the corridor and double-checked with the nurse. Not one mistake.
Keys, though. Still lost them yesterday.
Yamini

passage:
You want to know what changed in my first year as a sous-chef, Manoj? I'll tell you.
My name is Chinmay. On a busy night I've got twelve orders in my head, each with changes. No onion for table four. Extra spice for six. Table nine's allergic to nuts.
Two years ago I'd freeze. I'd drop one order to fix another. The head chef shouted at me every night.
Now I hold them differently. I group them: all the grills together, all the curries. I say each change out loud as I plate. I keep one line in my head for the allergies, like a red alarm.
Last Saturday the head chef watched me run the pass for an hour and said nothing. That's his version of praise.

qa.q: Which table was allergic to nuts?
qa.a: Table nine.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel on busy nights two years ago?
qa.a: Chinmay felt overwhelmed and frozen, dropping one order to fix another.

qa.q: What methods help Chinmay manage many orders at once?
qa.a: Grouping similar dishes, saying each change out loud, and keeping a separate mental line for allergies.

qa.q: How might the head chef see Chinmay now?
qa.a: He seems to trust Chinmay more, since his silence is a form of praise.

grounding: A young adult describes growing ability to hold and juggle complex information on the fly.

passage:
I'm Rafiq, and I share an office with Jasleen at the airline's ground desk.
Last Friday, a storm grounded four flights at once. Passengers crowded the counter. The screens kept freezing.
Jasleen didn't. She was on the phone with the crew desk, talking to a family whose child was unwell, and rebooking a group of students, all at once. She'd say, "Seat 14 goes to the mother, the students go on the 9 p.m., the elderly man gets the hotel voucher," and write almost nothing.
Later I asked her how she kept track. She shrugged. "I just hold it." Her hands were shaking a little when she said it.
I don't know what was going on in her head. From the outside, it looked like juggling fire.

qa.q: How many flights were grounded?
qa.a: Four flights.

qa.q: What might Jasleen have been feeling, given her shaking hands?
qa.a: She may have felt tense and drained under the calm surface, holding it all together.

qa.q: What could the airline do to support staff like Jasleen in such moments?
qa.a: Give clearer backup systems and a short break after the rush, so staff are not carrying everything in their heads.

qa.q: How does Rafiq see Jasleen's performance?
qa.a: Rafiq is impressed and a little amazed, though Rafiq admits not knowing what was going on in her head.

grounding: A colleague observes a young adult juggling complex information during a crisis.

passage:
Tuesday
Today the client changed the whole brief an hour before our presentation. New audience, new budget, new colours.
A year ago I'd have panicked and argued. Payal, my team lead, even looked at me like she expected that.
Instead I said, "Give me twenty minutes." I kept the structure we had, cut three slides, swapped the examples to fit the new audience, and changed the colours.
My hands were cold the whole time. It wasn't perfect. But the client nodded through most of it.
After, Payal said, "You bent without breaking. Nice." I felt ridiculously proud.
Note to self: the plan is not the goal. The goal is the goal.
Divyansh

qa.q: How long before the presentation did the client change the brief?
qa.a: An hour before.

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel after Payal's comment?
qa.a: Divyansh felt ridiculously proud, after being nervous with cold hands.

qa.q: What did Divyansh do that showed flexibility?
qa.a: Divyansh kept the useful structure and changed only what the new brief needed, instead of starting over or arguing.

qa.q: How might Payal have felt as the client nodded along?
qa.a: Payal probably felt relieved and pleased, having expected Divyansh to panic.

grounding: A young adult's diary showing quick adaptation when the rules of a task changed.

passage:
Lokesh had been running his father's grain shop in their small town for a year, keeping the old ledger system his father trusted. Then the wholesale market started accepting only digital payments.
His father refused. "We've done it this way for thirty years."
Lokesh felt stuck between them. He spent a week learning the new system from his friend Rashmi, who ran the stationery shop next door. He kept the ledger too, writing each digital payment in it, so his father could still read everything.
At first his father grumbled. After a month, he started checking the phone himself.
Rashmi teased, "You're good at bending both ways."
Lokesh shrugged. "The shop has to survive. So do we."

qa.a: For a year.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel when his father refused the change?
qa.a: He felt stuck and torn between his father and the new rules.

qa.q: What made Lokesh's solution work?
qa.a: He learned the new system but kept the old ledger alongside it, so his father could follow and slowly accept the change.

qa.q: How might Lokesh's father feel after a month?
qa.a: His father may feel less threatened and a bit curious, since he starts checking the phone himself.

grounding: Shows a young adult adapting smoothly when business rules suddenly change.
